title: Deterministic benchmark schedule and priming cookbook
content:
Purpose and scope:
This is a practical cookbook for creating deterministic (repeatable) throughput benchmarks against the serving runtime. The goal is not to produce the single best throughput number, but to produce numbers that are stable, explainable, and comparable across commits/hardware/model variants.

Context / why this exists:
We kept getting noisy throughput regressions where different runs produced ±10–20% throughput variance. Root causes were mixed: inconsistent warmup/priming, uncontrolled token pacing on clients, intermittent garbage collection on host-side helper processes, and different batch-formation timing. This doc consolidates a deterministic schedule, priming procedures, and analysis steps to reduce variance and surface real regressions.

High-level strategy (cookbook overview):
1) Fix the workload (seeded prompts, deterministic token lengths, locked RNGs).
2) Prime the runtime with a controlled sequence that populates caches in a predictable way.
3) Run a scheduled experiment with explicit measurement windows and a post-facto warmup-detection step.
4) Collect a broad telemetry set (latency histograms, batch-size distribution, KV hit ratio, GPU metrics).
5) Use repeat-run statistics (n>=6) + bootstrap CI to decide signal vs noise.

Testbed assumptions and minimum requirements:
- Model binary/artifact pinned (git tag or model sha).
- Serving runtime version pinned; include commit hash in test metadata.
- Hardware: report exact GPU model, driver, CUDA, cuDNN versions.
- Network: tests run on isolated test VLAN with capacity headroom >2x expected throughput.
- Load generator: use bench-harness v0.12+ (or our internal loadgen) with deterministic pacing options.

Workload creation (deterministic payloads):
- Use a small corpus of synthetic prompts (store as one-per-line file) and rotate through them deterministically rather than sampling. Example file: seeds/priming-100.txt
- Fix sequence length distributions. For variable-length tests, precompute a length schedule (e.g., 40% 32 tokens, 40% 64 tokens, 20% 256 tokens) and apply it as a circular schedule.
- Lock RNGs used by token sampling (both on client side if using sampling, and any model-side stochastic layers). Prefer deterministic decoding (greedy or beam with fixed seed) for throughput runs.

Priming / cache warmup recipe (deterministic priming schedule):
- Rationale: simple "fire X requests" warmup is fragile: different arrival patterns produce different KV cache reuse. We use a small, repeatable priming schedule to build stable cache footprint and kernel warm paths.
- Priming sequence (recommended):
  1) Cold start: send 10 requests spaced 50ms apart to ensure process start and JIT/kernels load.
  2) Short bursts: 5 bursts of 40 requests at the target concurrency, 1s apart. This forces typical batching behavior and populates KV caches.
  3) Long prefix: send 200 requests at 60% of target throughput paced evenly to load page tables and prefetch GPU memory paths.
  4) Quiet period: 30s sleep to allow metrics to settle, flush ephemeral buffers if needed.
- Note: numbers above are a starting point; capture priming-phase metrics and record them with the run.

Deterministic pacing and arrival model:
- Use client-side token pacing rather than firing full requests immediately. Measure two arrival patterns: Poisson (for realistic burstiness) and regular (deterministic inter-arrival). For repeatability, store the exact inter-arrival times used in each run.
- Recommended: for throughput regression checks, prefer deterministic inter-arrival times (constant interval) — this reduces arrival-induced variance.

Measurement windows and warmup detection algorithm:
- We record per-request timestamped tokens-served and latency. Measurement windows are aligned to wall-clock: "priming" window (excluded from final metrics), "ramp" window (optional), "steady-state" window (used for final metrics).
- Automatic warmup detection: run a sliding-window slope test on tokens/sec with window size W=30s and step S=5s. Consider steady state reached when the slope of tokens/sec over last 3 windows is within ±1% and CV < 2.5%. If not reached in max T=600s, fail the run (or record as non-converged). This algorithm gives an objective way to trim the initial transient.

Run orchestration and recommended durations:
- Minimum run duration (excluding priming): 300s steady-state measurement.
- Repeat count: at least 6 independent runs (fresh priming each time) for a given commit/config. Use same random seed schedule across runs to reduce cross-run variability.

Telemetry to capture (must be time-series and request-granular where possible):
- Request: request_id, start_ts, end_ts, tokens_produced, batch_size, kv_cache_hit (bool or ratio), decode_steps, queue_time_ms.
- Runtime: avg_batch_size, batch_size_histogram, queue_length, scheduling_delay_ms, memory_allocs, GC/pool-reclaims.
- Host/GPU: GPU util %, GPU memory used, SM efficiency (if available), PCIe bandwidth counters, CPU load, IRQ wait.
- OS: interrupts, context switches, dmesg warnings.
- Profiling: occasional nsys traces sampled (one per 10 runs) to capture kernel shapes and queue delays.

Analysis and metrics reporting:
- Primary metrics: tokens/sec (throughput), p50/p90/p99 latency for full response, mean batch size, KV cache hit rate.
- Report median across runs and 95% bootstrap CI. Also report CV across runs.
- For regression detection: require effect size > 3x standard error and absolute difference > 2% tokens/sec to declare a meaningful regression (tunable threshold).
- Produce time-series plots with measurement windows annotated and batch-size vs tokens/sec scatter plots.

Failure modes and checks (quick checklist):
- Check that priming completed (priming waveform matches historical baseline).
- If steady-state not reached, examine batch-size distribution and queue length spikes.
- Inspect GPU power throttling warnings and host-side OOM events.
- Confirm loadgen and runtime clocks aligned (NTP/skew can affect windowing).

Operational tips / gotchas:
- Avoid running other noisy tenants on the same host during microbenchmarks; background cronjobs or container scanners cause spikes.
- If using autoscaling in Dedicated, pin scaling to capacity to avoid dynamic node churn during a run.
- For variable-length workloads, a single long-running request can skew p99; consider truncation policy for consistent p99 comparisons.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Experiment with synthetic microbursts that emulate real customer mixes (we need a corpus from product telemetry).
- Evaluate if a hardware-level synchronization (e.g., flushed caches) before priming reduces cross-run variance.
- Add per-request kernel-stack sampling to correlate specific slow requests with kernel shapes.

Quick start commands (bench-harness examples):
- Priming + deterministic run (pseudo):
  bench-harness --model-tag v1.3.2 --seeds seeds/priming-100.txt --arrival-schedule schedules/const-interval-10ms.json --priming-cookbook-mode priming-cookbook.json --measure-window 300s --run-id $(git rev-parse --short HEAD)-$(date +%Y%m%d%H%M)

Notes on documentation and traceability:
- Each run MUST attach: model sha, runtime sha, gpu/driver versions, bench-harness git ref, loadgen config file, priming schedule file, and raw per-request CSV. Store these with artifacts in the bench-bucket and link in the run metadata.

Appendix: short example CSV line (per-request)
- run_id,request_id,start_ts,end_ts,tokens,batch_size,kv_hit,queue_ms,gpu_util
- r123,req-0001,1700000000.100,1700000000.310,128,8,0.75,2.3,72.1

If you run into flaky results, paste the priming waveform + batch-size histogram into #runtime-bench and tag me (jordan.p).
